title: Very slow join on small table (bad choice of join algorithm?)
body:
### What happens?

Very slow join on a small table.

This is extracted from a larger query on a multi-billion row table. The performance behavior can be observed at any scale though.

### To Reproduce

See attached zip:  [slow.zip](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/files/13720913/slow.zip)


```sql
SELECT t1.col1
FROM read_parquet('slow3.parquet') AS t1
LEFT JOIN read_parquet('slow3.parquet') AS t2
    ON t1.col1 = t2.col1
    -- The following condition is always false on the reproducer dataset.
    -- On the real world dataset, it is sometimes false.
    AND t1.col1 = 'missing'
GROUP BY t1.col1
```

Timing (small/large):

DuckDB: 9/35 s
chdb: 15/20 ms


NB: I don't know how to write the query above in Polars, but here are timing for a query without `AND t1.col1 = 'missing'`:

DuckDB: 10 s / 40 s
chdb: 1.5 s / 23 s
Polars (code below): 7 s / OOM

```py
df = pl.scan_parquet("slow3.parquet")
df.join(df, on=["col1"], how="left").select(pl.col.col1).group_by(pl.col.col1).agg().collect()
```

#### Note

The queries and timings above are a simplified example. My real world query is a bit more complicated:

```sql
SELECT t1.col1
FROM ... AS t1
LEFT JOIN ... AS t2
    ON t1.col1 = t2.col1
    AND t1.col2 IN (... small list of const strings ...)
    AND t2.col3 IN (... another small list of const strings ...)
GROUP BY t1.col1
```

### OS:

macOS, Linux

### DuckDB Version:

0.9.2

### DuckDB Client:

CLI

### Full Name:

Jonas Haag

### Affiliation:

QuantCo

### Have you tried this on the latest `main` branch?

I have tested with a release build (and could not test with a main build)

### Have you tried the steps to reproduce? Do they include all relevant data and configuration? Does the issue you report still appear there?

- [X] Yes, I have

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Hi @reporter,

I'm not sure what has already been mentioned since the thread history has been cleaned up, so sorry if I'm repeating anything you have already read/tried.

It seems there is a bug in DuckDB, and the filter `AND t1.col1 = 'missing'` is not being recognized as a standalone filter that can be pushed down. This causes DuckDB to plan a blockwise join instead of a  hash join, which is *much* slower. A simple workaround for this is to re-write the query as 

```
SELECT t1.col1
FROM read_parquet('slow3.parquet') AS t1
LEFT JOIN read_parquet('slow3.parquet') AS t2
    ON t1.col1 = t2.col1
    Where t1.col1 = 'missing'
GROUP BY t1.col1
```

This should speed up the execution time quite a bit since a hash join is used instead of a blockwise nested loop join.

I will be looking into fixing the issue as is though, I will let you know when it gets merged!

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Ok, I think I found a work around that gives you the same results. You just need to add the filter `t2.col1 = 'missing'`. This won't affect the result since the filter `t1.col1 = t2.col1` provides the transitivity. There is a significant speedup since t2 is  filtered down so that only matching tuples are compared during the join operation instead of all combinations of tuples. The query below gives you the same results and executes faster using the given data

```
SELECT t1.col1
FROM read_parquet('slow3.parquet') AS t1
LEFT JOIN read_parquet('slow3.parquet') AS t2
    ON t1.col1 = t2.col1
    AND t1.col1 = 'missing'
    AND t2.col1 = 'missing'
GROUP BY t1.col1;
```

If you want to make it even faster, removing the `t1.col1 = 'missing'` from the query above allows the optimizer to plan a hash group by  operator for the join.

```
SELECT t1.col1
FROM read_parquet('slow3.parquet') AS t1
LEFT JOIN read_parquet('slow3.parquet') AS t2
    ON t1.col1 = t2.col1
    AND t2.col1 = 'missing'
GROUP BY t1.col1;
```

Let me know if this works for you, I saw a speedup of about 9 seconds to 0.01 seconds. I'll look into implementing similar functionality in DuckDB, it should be doable, but I can't guarantee when it'll be merged

comments.body:
Hi Jonas,

Hmm, yes. The real world query does indeed make this problem harder to solve, as the string comparison for `t1.col2 = missing` makes the planner incorrectly think that a nested loop join should be used. 

Another workaround that might help speed things up requires that comparisons are always constant strings. A query like the one below *should* speed up your query,

```
 select * exclude some_tmp_name 
 from read_parquet('slow2.parquet') t1 left join 
(select *, 'missing2' some_tmp_name from read_parquet('slow3.parquet')) t2 on 
  t1.col1 = t2.col1 and 
  t1.col2 = t2.some_tmp_name and 
  t2.col3 = 'missing'
group by t1.col1;
 ```

This helps the optimizer recognize that the comparison `t1.col2 = missing` can also be done using a hash table. 

Let me know if this works! It won't provide much speed up with the reproducible files you gave me, but maybe in your real world data set it will 👍

comments.body:
Thank you, this sort of works, but has serious limitations:

1. You need to write it this way:

   ```sql
   SELECT ...
   FROM (SELECT * FROM ..., 'missing3' as const3) t1
   LEFT JOIN (SELECT * FROM ..., 'missing2' as const2) t2
   ON t1.col1 = t2.col1
   AND t1.col2 = missing2
   AND t2.col3 = missing3
   ```

   but not this way (with the constant values in each side's "own" SELECT):

   ```sql
   SELECT ...
   FROM (SELECT * FROM ..., 'missing2' as const2) t1
   LEFT JOIN (SELECT * FROM ..., 'missing3' as const3) t2
   ON t1.col1 = t2.col1
   AND t1.col2 = missing2
   AND t2.col3 = missing3
   ```
2. It does not work with my real world query because there we don't have `col = missing` but `col IN (missing_1, missing_2, ...)`. It also doesn't work with `(col = missing_1 OR col = missing_2 ...)`. Sorry that I didn't include this fact in my reduced example either.

With the `=` instead of `IN` it gives a at least 50x speedup (I didn't wait for the NL join query to finish)

comments.author: participant5
comments.body:
If I'm understanding the conversation so far correctly, it seems there are a few separate things going on here:
* In the original (simple) query, it's possible to propagate the constant equality through transitivity which opens up opportunities for optimization by recognizing the key is absent on the right side of the join. This propagation is currently not done automatically, but it would likely be possible to do so and some queries would benefit from this.
* The constant string comparison in the join clause prevents DuckDB from using a hash join even if a hash join could work for the query. A blockwise nested loop join is used instead and is slower.
* The query without the constant string equality (i.e. simple join followed by group) is still about 6 times slower on a small dataset than a similar query in chdb. This query _does_ use a hash join in DuckDB.

I have some time and appetite to work on this (though not promising I'll be successful). I'd like to narrow it down to a more specific issue though. The constraint propagation seems like it would be relatively straightforward to add but doesn't solve the problem for the more complicated query and wouldn't help @participant4 either.

@reporter I do think a reproducer dataset for the more complex query could be useful, especially in combination with EXPLAIN ANALYZE outputs both on DuckDB and chdb. Then I'd be happy to look into what's driving the performance differences you're running into, and what changes can be made.

comments.author: participant6
comments.body:
Hi, I also ran into this issue as well.
The planner goes with blockwise when there are more than two conditionals on the `ON`.

For my use case, the workaround was to simply break up the join condition, join the righthand table multiple times and then coalesce the final value.

Example to repo the issue and demonstrate the workaround.
```sql
CREATE TABLE lhs_big_table AS 
SELECT 
    DATE '2000-01-01' + (random() * 8766)::INTEGER AS date1,
    DATE '2010-01-01' + (random() * 8766)::INTEGER AS date2,
    DATE '2021-01-01' + (random() * 8767)::INTEGER AS date3 
FROM generate_series(1, 10000000);


CREATE TABLE rhs_small_table AS 
SELECT 
    DATE '2000-01-01' + (random() * 8766)::INTEGER AS small_date1,
    DATE '2010-01-01' + (random() * 8766)::INTEGER AS small_date2,
    DATE '2021-01-01' + (random() * 8767)::INTEGER AS small_date3 
FROM generate_series(1, 100);

-- Single complex join
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT small_date2
FROM lhs_big_table
    LEFT JOIN rhs_small_table ON lhs_big_table.date1 = rhs_small_table.small_date1
    AND ((
            lhs_big_table.date2 = rhs_small_table.small_date2
            AND lhs_big_table.date3 < rhs_small_table.small_date3
        )
        OR (
            lhs_big_table.date2 < rhs_small_table.small_date2
        )
    )
;

-- Two simple joins
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT COALESCE(rhs_one.small_date2, rhs_two.small_date2) AS small_date2
FROM lhs_big_table
    LEFT JOIN rhs_small_table rhs_one ON lhs_big_table.date1 = rhs_one.small_date1
    AND (
        lhs_big_table.date2 = rhs_one.small_date2
        AND lhs_big_table.date3 < rhs_one.small_date3
    )
    LEFT JOIN rhs_small_table rhs_two ON lhs_big_table.date1 = rhs_two.small_date1
    AND (
        lhs_big_table.date2 < rhs_two.small_date2
    )
;

-- Confirming the queries are equivalent
WITH table_one AS (
    SELECT small_date2
    FROM lhs_big_table
        LEFT JOIN rhs_small_table ON lhs_big_table.date1 = rhs_small_table.small_date1
        AND ((
                lhs_big_table.date2 = rhs_small_table.small_date2
                AND lhs_big_table.date3 < rhs_small_table.small_date3
            )
            OR (
                lhs_big_table.date2 < rhs_small_table.small_date2
            )
        )
),
table_two AS (
    SELECT COALESCE(rhs_one.small_date2, rhs_two.small_date2) AS small_date2
    FROM lhs_big_table
        LEFT JOIN rhs_small_table rhs_one ON lhs_big_table.date1 = rhs_one.small_date1
        AND (
            lhs_big_table.date2 = rhs_one.small_date2
            AND lhs_big_table.date3 < rhs_one.small_date3
        )
        LEFT JOIN rhs_small_table rhs_two ON lhs_big_table.date1 = rhs_two.small_date1
        AND (
            lhs_big_table.date2 < rhs_two.small_date2
        )
)
SELECT 
    CASE 
        WHEN COUNT(*) = 0 THEN 'Tables are identical'
        ELSE 'Tables are different'
    END AS comparison_result
FROM (
    (SELECT * FROM table_one
    EXCEPT
    SELECT * FROM table_two)
    UNION ALL
    (SELECT * FROM table_two
    EXCEPT
    SELECT * FROM table_one)
) AS diff;
```
